title: A default parameter supplies a value when its argument is omitted
body: In a function definition, parameter=default specifies the value used when the corresponding argument is omitted from a call.
detail: With def greet(name='user'), calling greet() uses 'user' for name. Calling greet('Mina') supplies an explicit argument, so that value is used instead of the default. Read the default in the definition together with whether the call provides that argument.
examples: With def search(limit=5), search() uses limit=5.
search(limit=20) uses the explicitly supplied value 20.

title: elif is tested only after earlier branches have been false
body: An if/elif/else chain checks conditions from top to bottom, executes the first matching branch, and skips the remaining branches.
detail: An elif condition is reached only when the earlier branches were not selected. Read each condition in order and stop once the first true branch is selected. An optional else handles the case where every preceding condition is false.
examples: elif status == 'retry' is checked only if the preceding if was false.
elif not items: is reached only after earlier states were not selected.

title: The else clause of try runs only when the try suite finishes without an exception
body: In try/except/else, the else block runs when the try block completes normally without raising an exception.
detail: If the try block raises a handled exception, execution moves to except and skips else. When try completes normally, except is skipped and else runs. An exception raised inside the else block is not handled by the preceding except clauses.
examples: Use a parsed JSON result in else only when parsing succeeded.
If try raises ValueError, the matching except runs and else is skipped.

title: PureWindowsPath combines path segments using Windows path rules
body: PureWindowsPath(*segments) creates a Windows-flavoured pure path from path segments without accessing the filesystem.
detail: PureWindowsPath can represent Windows paths on any operating system. PureWindowsPath('.venv', 'Scripts', 'Activate.ps1') combines the three arguments as path components. Constructing the object does not check whether the file exists or open the file.
examples: PureWindowsPath('.venv', 'Scripts', 'Activate.ps1')
str(PureWindowsPath('C:/Temp', 'a.txt')) returns its string representation.

title: list2cmdline converts an argument sequence to a Windows command-line string
body: subprocess.list2cmdline(sequence) converts a sequence of command arguments into one Windows command-line string.
detail: It does not execute the command. Read the sequence as program name, subcommand, options, and values in order. Arguments that require quoting can be represented according to Windows command-line quoting rules.
examples: A list beginning with winget, install, and --id preserves that argument order.
The result of list2cmdline(parts) is a command string, not process output.

title: from-import binds selected names from a module into the current namespace
body: from module import name finds and loads the module, then binds the requested name in the current scope.
detail: In from .config import DATA_DIR, TOP_K, .config is the source module and DATA_DIR and TOP_K are the imported names. A leading dot denotes a relative import from the current package. The imported names can then be used without the module prefix.
examples: from pathlib import Path binds Path in the current module.
from .config import DATA_DIR, TOP_K imports two names from a relative module.

title: pd.concat combines pandas objects along a selected axis
body: pandas.concat(objs, axis=...) concatenates multiple Series or DataFrame objects along an axis.
detail: The default axis=0 commonly stacks rows. With ignore_index=True, the existing labels on the concatenation axis are not used and a new zero-based index is created. Read the input objects together with axis and ignore_index.
examples: pd.concat([df_old, df_new], ignore_index=True) combines both DataFrames with a new index.
axis=1 concatenates along the column direction.

title: pivot_table creates a summarized table from grouping keys and an aggregation rule
body: DataFrame.pivot_table() groups data using index or columns and aggregates values using aggfunc.
detail: index selects the row grouping key, values chooses what to aggregate, and aggfunc selects the aggregation such as mean or sum. df.pivot_table(index='domain', values='score', aggfunc='mean') therefore computes average score by domain.
examples: index='domain' groups result rows by domain.
aggfunc='mean' calculates the mean of the selected values in each group.

title: Passwords are stored as password hashes rather than plaintext
body: Password hashing transforms a password into a protected one-way representation intended for storage and later verification.
detail: Code such as hasher.hash(plain_password) should be read as producing the stored password-hash representation. This is different from Python's general hash() operation or using a fast general-purpose hash directly for password storage. Authentication verifies a supplied password against the stored representation rather than decrypting the password.
examples: password_hash = hasher.hash(plain_password)
Store a password hash rather than the plaintext password.

title: Developer logs and user-facing error messages serve different audiences
body: Developer logs record events and diagnostic information, while user-facing messages explain the problem safely and help the user decide what to do next.
detail: The same failure may send useful debugging detail to log_error(...) while show_error(...) displays a concise message without exposing internal stack traces or secrets. Read these as separate diagnostic and UI output paths.
examples: log_error(error_detail) records information for investigation.
show_error('Something went wrong') gives the user a concise message.

title: Using a sqlite connection with with creates a transaction success/failure boundary
body: When a sqlite3 Connection is used as a context manager, an open transaction is committed on successful exit and rolled back when an uncaught exception leaves the block.
detail: Using with conn: does not automatically close the connection, and the context manager does not necessarily open a new transaction by itself. For migration code, read the SQL statements inside the block as a success-or-failure transaction boundary.
examples: Successful statements inside with conn: may be committed when the block exits.
If an exception escapes the block, an open transaction is rolled back.

title: A secret that must later be recovered can be encrypted before storage
body: A secret such as an API key can be transformed from plaintext into ciphertext before it is persisted when the original value must later be recoverable.
detail: Read encrypted = encrypt(api_key) followed by upsert_secret(encrypted) as protecting the plaintext before the storage call. Encryption differs from password hashing because the original data can be recovered with the correct key, so the encryption key must be protected separately from the ciphertext.
examples: encrypted = encrypt(api_key)
upsert_secret(encrypted) stores the encrypted representation rather than plaintext.
